content_preview.title: Unsealed Filings Show Microsoft Executive Called AI Training Data Scraping 'the Largest Theft of Labor in Human History'
content_preview.summary: Newly unredacted filings in the NYT v. OpenAI and Microsoft copyright suit quote a Microsoft director calling AI scraping practices theft and OpenAI's ChatGPT head calling them an existential threat to publishers.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Newly unredacted material in the copyright lawsuit The New York Times brought against OpenAI and Microsoft three years ago includes internal statements in which a top Microsoft executive privately described the companies' AI training practices as "theft," while OpenAI's own leadership said its AI models posed an "existential threat" to the publishers and journalists whose work trained them, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/17/microsoft-exec-called-ai-scraping...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News-category piece using the standard Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know format. Clear, neutral prose; every paragraph in 'What We Know' is source-attributed inline. Word count (829) is within the News 400-1200 range.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read both source snapshots in full from sources/2026-09/unsealed-filings-show-microsoft-executive-called-ai-training-data-scraping-the-largest-theft-of-labor-in-human-history/ (gunzip'd, not re-fetched). Verified sha256 of both decompressed files matches the manifest (source-0.html.gz = d287d319..., source-1.html.gz = d2c1b20b...), confirming snapshot integrity. Neither source has a suspicious_patterns entry in manifest.json (both null). source-0.html.gz (TechCrunch, Rebecca Bellan, 'Microsoft exec called AI scraping the largest theft of labor in human history, new unredacted filings reveal', published 2026-09-17): read the full extracted body text. This is the primary source for nearly every claim/quote in the article and it independently supports all of them verbatim, including: Brent Hecht (identified as 'Microsoft's director of Applied Science') calling the practices 'an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions' and 'the largest theft of labor in human history' in a January 2023 memo; the 'doom loop' quote from a January 2024 Hecht presentation; the 93% Copilot/Bing click-through-rate drop; the 'It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens...' Microsoft document quote; Nick Turley (OpenAI head of ChatGPT) calling AI products an 'existential threat' to publishers that are 'largely substitutive' and 'will get more and more substitutive as they get better'; Greg Brockman calling models 'excellent at news'; Satya Nadella's deposition quotes on paywalled licensing and substitution; the Nick Ryder / Brockman 'hack to get around nytimes paywall' / 'ah nice' exchange (Nick Ryder is named in this source); the 91,692-copies and 2-million-document figures; the 'OpenAI delivered the entire GPT-3 training dataset to Microsoft' and Project Taxi/Project Mango quotes and the 160,903-unique-works figure; the Steven Lieberman (NY Daily News counsel) quote; and the framing that quotes come from NYT's brief rather than sealed exhibits, and that other AI-copyright judges have leaned toward fair use. source-1.html.gz (Engadget, Steve Dent, archive.org fallback snapshot dated 2026-09-18, live URL had returned 200 but archive fallback was used per manifest): read in full. Independently confirms Hecht's 'largest theft of labor in human history' quote with the same 'director of Applied Science' title, the 'doom loop' reference, Turley's 'existential threat to publishers' and 'largely substitutive' characterizations, the Brockman 'ah nice' exchange (though Engadget does not name Nick Ryder as the employee -- the article correctly cites TechCrunch, which does name him, as the source for that attribution and cites Engadget only as independent corroboration of the exchange itself), and the Alex Haurek/Microsoft spokesperson statement. One minor note: the article's Haurek quote ('Microsoft's position is set out in its court filings, which explain why these transformative uses are consistent with copyright law') is a truncation of Engadget's full quote, which continues '...and why Copilot is not a substitute for publishers' journalism.' The words used are exact and in order, and the closing quotation mark is placed correctly at the truncation point -- this is a standard partial quotation, not a misquote or fabrication, and does not change the meaning of the portion quoted.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No hallucinated quotes or fabricated specifics found. Every direct quote, name, title, date, and figure checked against the raw snapshot text was verbatim and correctly attributed. The striking 'largest theft of labor in human history' quote was independently verified in both sources with consistent attribution to Brent Hecht, Microsoft's director of Applied Science, in a January 2023 internal memo -- exactly as the article states. Nick Turley's 'existential threat' and 'largely substitutive' quotes are equally well corroborated across both outlets.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional. The piece reports the filings' contents and quotes without editorializing, includes Microsoft's disavowal of its own employee's statements, and closes with an appropriately hedged 'What We Don't Know' section noting the quotes lack full context and that other courts have leaned toward fair use.

concerns: The Alex Haurek/Microsoft spokesperson quote is truncated mid-sentence relative to Engadget's full quote, though the truncation does not alter the meaning of the portion quoted and the quotation marks are placed correctly at the cut point -- not significant enough to warrant a correction.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Strong, well-sourced News piece. Both cited sources were read in full from disk, sha256-verified against the manifest, and independently corroborate the article's central and most consequential claims, including the striking direct quote attributed to Brent Hecht and the Nick Turley 'existential threat' characterization that received extra scrutiny per the review brief. The April 6, 2026 cross-reference is accurate and resolves to real, related prior coverage. No fabrications, no misattributions, no bidirectional source-array gaps, no suspicious-pattern findings.
